title: MultiStructRNA: a Python package for multi-algorithm RNA secondary structure prediction, ensemble analysis, and visualization
summary: We introduce MultiStructRNA, a unified Python toolkit for RNA secondary structure prediction, ensemble analysis, and visualization. Although RNA secondary structure is central to RNA biology and therapeutic design, practical adoption is often hindered by fragmented tooling, incompatible input and output formats, and limited visualization support. MultiStructRNA addresses these challenges through a single high-level API that orchestrates multiple prediction algorithms, harmonizes results into a consistent schema, and provides reproducible, ensemble-aware metrics through an object model suited to both interactive notebooks and production pipelines. MultiStructRNA enables seamless switching between prediction methods without requiring workflow changes and supports both in-notebook and exportable visualizations. Designed for scalability, it supports high-throughput analyses and simplifies comparison across methods while standardizing downstream feature extraction. The current release also includes optional agent-readable workflow recipes that document dependency setup, backend-adapter conventions, SHAPE-data reconciliation, structure interpretation, and comparative sequence analyses. By integrating diverse RNA secondary structure packages within a common framework, MultiStructRNA streamlines structure analysis and facilitates its use in RNA design, optimization, and machine learning workflows.

AI.tldr: MultiStructRNA is a unified Python toolkit for RNA secondary structure prediction, ensemble analysis, and visualization, providing a single high-level API that orchestrates multiple prediction algorithms, harmonizes results into a consistent schema, and offers reproducible, ensemble-aware metrics suitable for both interactive notebooks and production pipelines.
AI.motivation: RNA secondary structure is central to RNA biology and therapeutic design, but practical adoption is hindered by fragmented tooling, incompatible input/output formats, and limited visualization support.
AI.method: MultiStructRNA provides a single high-level API that orchestrates multiple prediction algorithms, harmonizes results into a consistent schema, offers reproducible ensemble-aware metrics through an object model, supports seamless switching between prediction methods, provides in-notebook and exportable visualizations, and includes agent-readable workflow recipes for setup, backend conventions, SHAPE-data reconciliation, structure interpretation, and comparative analysis.
AI.result: The toolkit enables seamless switching between prediction methods without workflow changes, supports high-throughput analyses, simplifies cross-method comparison, and standardizes downstream feature extraction while offering both interactive and exportable visualizations.
AI.conclusion: By integrating diverse RNA secondary structure packages within a common framework, MultiStructRNA streamlines structure analysis and facilitates its use in RNA design, optimization, and machine learning workflows.

title: Social Discounting Enables Fast and Reliable Collective Escape
summary: Solitary animals face a tradeoff when detecting threats: faster detection means accepting more false alarms. We show that groups can manage this tradeoff better by treating an undisturbed neighbor as evidence against a threat, becoming both faster and more accurate than lone individuals. Modeling each animal as a noisy evidence-accumulator that flees when its belief crosses a threshold, we find that a neighbor's flight signals danger while its stillness signals safety. A naive responder reacts only to flights and inflates false alarms as the group grows; a Bayesian responder weighs both, approximated by a single social discounting rate that interpolates between these limits. This yields closed-form expressions for group performance, including cascade branching ratios that stay strongly subcritical in safety and turn supercritical under threat, so the rate at which an animal discounts a threat while its neighbors stay still can be inferred from behavior alone, and it sets a ceiling on how many neighbors an animal can attend before discounting alone can no longer hold its false-alarm rate. Wild sulphur molly shoals under bird attack are best described by discounting rates well above what individually Bayesian updating supplies over any neighborhood they could plausibly attend, and the same model, at the inferred value, predicts a false-alarm rate that stays constant as shoals grow.

AI.tldr: Groups can outperform solitary animals in threat detection by using undisturbed neighbors as evidence of safety, balancing speed and accuracy. A Bayesian social-evidence model explains how neighbors' stillness discounts threats, yields closed-form group performance predictions, and matches wild sulphur molly shoal behavior under bird attack.
AI.motivation: Solitary animals face a speed-accuracy tradeoff in threat detection—faster detection leads to more false alarms. The paper asks whether groups can resolve this tradeoff better than individuals by leveraging social information beyond just flight responses.
AI.method: Models each animal as a noisy evidence-accumulator that flees when belief crosses a threshold. A neighbor's flight signals danger while stillness signals safety. Compares a naive responder (reacts only to flights, inflating false alarms) to a Bayesian responder (weighs both signals), approximated by a single social discounting rate. Derives closed-form expressions for group performance and cascade branching ratios.
AI.result: Branching ratios stay strongly subcritical in safety and turn supercritical under threat. The discounting rate can be inferred from behavior alone and sets a ceiling on attentional capacity. Wild sulphur molly shoals under bird attack show discounting rates well above individually Bayesian updating, and at the inferred value the model predicts false-alarm rates that stay constant as shoals grow.
AI.conclusion: Groups manage the detection tradeoff better than solitary individuals by treating stillness as evidence against a threat. The social discounting framework provides testable predictions and explains observed group behavior in natural predator-prey systems.

title: Synaptic delays modulate population phase and amplitude responses in oscillatory excitatory-inhibitory networks
summary: Synaptic delays are fundamental determinants of neuronal communication and can profoundly influence the emergence and stability of cortical oscillations. Although their role in shaping network synchronization is well established, how synaptic delays regulate the collective response of neuronal populations to transient perturbations remains poorly understood. Here, we investigate the effects of synaptic delays on the phase and amplitude responses of oscillatory activity in a conductance-based excitatory-inhibitory spiking network operating in the pyramidal-interneuron gamma (PING) regime. By systematically varying the synaptic delay and applying brief external perturbations to the excitatory population, inhibitory population, or the entire network, we computed network phase response curves (nPRCs) and network amplitude response curves (nARCs) to quantify changes in oscillation timing and population coherence. Increasing synaptic delay slowed network oscillations while enhancing population synchrony, demonstrating a trade-off between oscillation frequency and coherence. Excitatory perturbations produced relatively robust phase responses across delays but exhibited a pronounced delay-dependent reduction in amplitude enhancement. In contrast, inhibitory perturbations generated substantially stronger delay-dependent modulation of both phase resetting and amplitude suppression, whereas whole-network stimulation combined features of both excitatory and inhibitory responses. Taken toghether, these findings identify synaptic delay as a key parameter governing the balance between phase resetting and amplitude modulation and provide a computational framework for understanding delay-dependent control of oscillatory brain networks.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how synaptic delays affect the phase and amplitude responses of oscillatory activity in a conductance-based excitatory-inhibitory spiking network operating in the PING (pyramidal-interneuron gamma) regime. Using network phase response curves (nPRCs) and network amplitude response curves (nARCs), the authors show that increasing synaptic delay slows oscillations while enhancing synchrony, and that different perturbation targets (excitatory, inhibitory, or whole network) exhibit distinct delay-dependent modulation of phase resetting and amplitude responses.
AI.motivation: While synaptic delays are known to shape network synchronization and the emergence/stability of cortical oscillations, their role in regulating how neuronal populations collectively respond to transient perturbations remains poorly understood. The paper aims to fill this gap.
AI.method: A conductance-based excitatory-inhibitory spiking network in the PING regime was used. Synaptic delays were systematically varied, and brief external perturbations were applied to the excitatory population, inhibitory population, or the entire network. Network phase response curves (nPRCs) and network amplitude response curves (nARCs) were computed to quantify changes in oscillation timing and population coherence.
AI.result: Increasing synaptic delay slowed network oscillations while enhancing population synchrony, revealing a trade-off between oscillation frequency and coherence. Excitatory perturbations yielded robust phase responses across delays but showed a pronounced delay-dependent reduction in amplitude enhancement. Inhibitory perturbations produced substantially stronger delay-dependent modulation of both phase resetting and amplitude suppression. Whole-network stimulation combined features of both response types.
AI.conclusion: Synaptic delay is a key parameter governing the balance between phase resetting and amplitude modulation in oscillatory networks, and the findings provide a computational framework for understanding delay-dependent control of oscillatory brain networks.

title: Phase- and amplitude-dependent control of synchronization in excitatory-inhibitory networks via pulsed stimulation
summary: Oscillatory neuronal networks exhibit complex collective responses to external perturbations that depend on both the intrinsic network dynamics and the timing of stimulation. Although phase response curves (PRCs) have become a standard tool for characterizing these responses, phase resetting alone provides an incomplete description of how transient perturbations reshape collective activity. Here, we investigate the dynamics of a balanced excitatory-inhibitory network of exponential integrate-and-fire (EIF) neurons subjected to phase-targeted current pulses. By jointly analyzing the network phase response curve (nPRC), network amplitude response curve (nARC), and changes in the population synchrony, we establish a framework for characterizing collective network responses in terms of phase, amplitude, and synchronization. We show that identical stimulation pulses can either enhance, suppress, or leave network synchronization unchanged depending solely on their phase within the oscillation cycle, revealing distinct synchronizing and desynchronizing windows. The nARC further identifies robust phase intervals that maximize suppression of oscillatory activity and provide optimal targets for repeated stimulation. Successive perturbations progressively desynchronize the network activity while continuously reshaping the phase, amplitude, and synchrony response landscapes, driving the network toward a modified dynamical state without altering the optimal stimulation phase. These cumulative effects remain robust across stimulation intensities, inhibitory synaptic time constants, and independent network realizations. Our results demonstrate that phase, amplitude, and synchronization represent complementary dynamical dimensions of oscillatory neuronal networks and provide general principles for the state-dependent control of collective dynamics through phase-targeted perturbations.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a framework for characterizing how oscillatory balanced excitatory-inhibitory networks of EIF neurons respond to phase-targeted current pulses, jointly analyzing network phase response curves (nPRC), amplitude response curves (nARC), and population synchrony to show that identical stimuli can enhance, suppress, or leave synchronization unchanged depending on stimulus phase, with cumulative stimulation progressively desynchronizing the network.
AI.motivation: While PRCs are standard tools for characterizing neuronal responses to perturbations, phase resetting alone provides an incomplete description of how transient perturbations reshape collective activity in oscillatory networks. A more comprehensive framework is needed to capture phase, amplitude, and synchrony dimensions of network responses.
AI.method: The authors simulate a balanced excitatory-inhibitory network of exponential integrate-and-fire (EIF) neurons and subject it to phase-targeted current pulses. They jointly compute the network phase response curve (nPRC), network amplitude response curve (nARC), and changes in population synchrony across different stimulation phases, also examining repeated stimulation and robustness across intensities, time constants, and network realizations.
AI.result: Identical stimulation pulses can enhance, suppress, or leave network synchronization unchanged depending solely on phase, revealing distinct synchronizing and desynchronizing windows. The nARC identifies phase intervals maximizing suppression of oscillatory activity for optimal repeated stimulation targeting. Successive perturbations progressively desynchronize the network while reshaping response landscapes toward a modified dynamical state without shifting the optimal stimulation phase. These effects are robust across intensities, synaptic time constants, and network realizations.
AI.conclusion: Phase, amplitude, and synchronization represent complementary dynamical dimensions of oscillatory neuronal networks, and the framework provides general principles for state-dependent control of collective dynamics through phase-targeted perturbations.

title: Valhalla: A Layered Knowledge-State and Service-Governance Framework for Long-Term Scientific Knowledge Work
summary: As large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly adopted in scientific research, external knowledge bases, knowledge graphs, and long-term memory have improved information retrieval and task continuity. However, most structured knowledge systems remain node-centric, representing files, concepts, results, and judgments as nodes and relations in a graph. While suitable for personal knowledge management, such structures often depend on individual organizational practices, limiting knowledge sharing, integration, and reorganization across users. This paper presents Valhalla, a layered knowledge-state and service-governance framework for long-term scientific knowledge work. Valhalla replaces flat graphs with layered encapsulation and stable semantic boundaries through a five-layer File-Resource-Entity-Relationship-Graph (FREG) model. File and Resource preserve source identity and provenance, Entity represents knowledge objects, Relationship captures semantic judgments, and Graph provides task-oriented knowledge views, enabling knowledge states from different researchers to be exchanged and reorganized under a unified structure. We further introduce a Router-Contract-Workflow service-governance architecture, inspired by the microkernel paradigm, to constrain how language models access, modify, and extend knowledge states while maintaining structural consistency and auditable operational boundaries. We implement a Valhalla prototype and validate knowledge ingestion, cross-member integration, and scientific writing support through an antibody-design review task comprising 26 paper resources, 80 knowledge entities, and 92 semantic relations. Rather than proposing a new knowledge-extraction algorithm, Valhalla offers a paradigm for organizing collaborative scientific knowledge, transforming individualized knowledge structures into transferable and reorganizable shared knowledge states.

AI.tldr: Valhalla is a layered knowledge-state and service-governance framework for long-term scientific knowledge work with LLM agents. It replaces node-centric flat graphs with a five-layer File-Resource-Entity-Relationship-Graph (FREG) model for stable semantic boundaries, and introduces a Router-Contract-Workflow architecture to govern how LLMs access and modify knowledge states. Validated on an antibody-design review task with 26 papers, 80 entities, and 92 relations.
AI.motivation: Existing structured knowledge systems for LLM agents are node-centric graph structures that rely on individual organizational practices, limiting knowledge sharing, integration, and reorganization across different researchers. There is a need for a unified structure that makes collaborative scientific knowledge transferable and reorganizable.
AI.method: The paper proposes Valhalla with two key components: (1) a five-layer FREG (File-Resource-Entity-Relationship-Graph) model that provides layered encapsulation—File/Resource preserve source provenance, Entity represents knowledge objects, Relationship captures semantic judgments, and Graph offers task-oriented views; and (2) a Router-Contract-Workflow service-governance architecture inspired by the microkernel paradigm to constrain how language models access, modify, and extend knowledge states while maintaining consistency and auditable boundaries.
AI.result: A Valhalla prototype was implemented and validated through an antibody-design review task comprising 26 paper resources, 80 knowledge entities, and 92 semantic relations, demonstrating knowledge ingestion, cross-member integration, and scientific writing support.
AI.conclusion: Valhalla offers a paradigm for organizing collaborative scientific knowledge rather than a new knowledge-extraction algorithm—transforming individualized knowledge structures into transferable and reorganizable shared knowledge states for long-term scientific work.

title: Phylogeny-based metrics of biodiversity: concepts and methods
summary:
The concept of valuing evolutionary history has a long tradition and was formalized by several research groups in the early 1990s, each aiming to capture the products of evolution more comprehensively than species richness alone. Preserving the "Tree of Life" has since become a central, if sometimes contested, goal in conservation biology. Faith's phylogenetic diversity (PD), defined as the sum of the edge lengths of a rooted tree connecting a set of focal entities, is the most widely used metric in this context and underpins an extensive methodological framework. This framework includes widely used species-specific indices such as EDGE, as well as approaches that quantify expected species-specific contributions to PD such as EDGE2.
  This chapter focuses on the development of this framework of phylogeny-based conservation metrics. We review the development of species-specific indices, highlighting their strengths and limitations, and trace their progression from simple formulations to game-theoretic approaches and more abstract generalizations. We also discuss how these indices are applied in conservation practice, with particular emphasis on the EDGE framework. We further discuss the relationship between the edge lengths of a phylogeny and the evolutionary features they are intended to represent. Finally, we highlight recent advances in the field and identify areas for future research.

AI.tldr: This chapter reviews the development of phylogeny-based conservation metrics, focusing on Faith's phylogenetic diversity (PD) and species-specific indices like EDGE and EDGE2, tracing their evolution from simple formulations to game-theoretic approaches, and discussing their applications, limitations, and future research directions.
AI.motivation: To comprehensively review the framework of phylogeny-based conservation metrics, from the foundational concept of PD to modern species-specific indices, highlighting their strengths, limitations, and applications in conservation practice.
AI.method: A literature review tracing the progression of species-specific conservation indices from early simple formulations through game-theoretic approaches to abstract generalizations, examining their practical applications (especially the EDGE framework) and the theoretical relationship between phylogeny edge lengths and evolutionary features.
AI.result: The chapter synthesizes the development of PD-based conservation metrics, documents the strengths and limitations of species-specific indices, and identifies recent advances and open questions in phylogeny-based conservation prioritization.
AI.conclusion: Phylogeny-based conservation metrics have evolved into a sophisticated framework, but there remain important gaps to address—including clarifying the link between edge lengths and actual evolutionary features, and further developing the theoretical foundations of these indices.

title: Stochastic Pharmacokinetic Escape: A Field-Theoretic Approach to Fluctuation-Induced Tumor Relapse
summary: Classical mathematical oncology employs deterministic mean-field models predicting that sufficiently high chemotherapy doses drive tumor density to zero. We show that this apparent cure is an artifact of neglecting demographic fluctuations. We construct a nonequilibrium stochastic PK-PD field theory combining a two-compartment pharmacokinetic model with a stochastic tumor-immune sector in the Doi-Peliti formalism, then map it to coupled multiplicative Langevin equations via the Martin-Siggia-Rose/Janssen-De Dominicis approach. In immune-depleted sanctuary sites, the dynamics reduce to a time-dependent Feller diffusion whose Fokker-Planck equation yields an analytical survival functional: demographic noise implies a strictly nonzero relapse probability for tumor micro-clusters under high-dose chemotherapy. Standard bolus administration acts as a nonselective annihilation process, driving immune fields into an absorbing state and creating a spatially immune-depleted vacuum that enables fluctuation-induced relapse -- Stochastic Pharmacokinetic Escape. We derive quantitative conditions under which metronomic dosing and adjuvant immunotherapy suppress this stochastic window of vulnerability. A model-agnostic analysis of 1461 longitudinal patient records shows that the majority of evaluable lesions exhibit a nadir followed by measurable regrowth rather than monotonic elimination; fitting the model's drift functional to these trajectories reproduces this pattern quantitatively, and a direct test of the predicted demographic-noise scaling law reveals size-dependent noise largest at the smallest observed tumor volumes, consistent with the proposed mechanism.

AI.tldr: This paper challenges the classical deterministic prediction that high-dose chemotherapy eliminates tumors, showing that demographic (stochastic) fluctuations necessarily create a nonzero relapse probability. Using a nonequilibrium stochastic PK-PD field theory, analytical solutions, and clinical data from 1461 patients, the authors demonstrate that chemotherapy can induce an immune-depleted vacuum enabling fluctuation-driven relapse ("Stochastic Pharmacokinetic Escape"), and derive conditions for metronomic dosing and immunotherapy to suppress it.
AI.motivation: Classical mathematical oncology uses deterministic mean-field models that predict high-dose chemotherapy drives tumor density to zero. The authors argue this "cure" is an artifact of neglecting demographic fluctuations, and seek to reveal a fundamentally stochastic mechanism of relapse that deterministic models cannot capture.
AI.method: The authors construct a nonequilibrium stochastic PK-PD field theory combining a two-compartment pharmacokinetic model with a stochastic tumor-immune sector using the Doi-Peliti formalism. This is mapped to coupled multiplicative Langevin equations via the Martin-Siggia-Rose/Janssen-De Dominicis approach. In immune-depleted sanctuary sites, the dynamics reduce to a time-dependent Feller diffusion whose Fokker-Planck equation yields an analytical survival functional. They validate against 1461 longitudinal patient records and test the demographic-noise scaling law.
AI.result: Demographic noise guarantees a strictly nonzero relapse probability for tumor micro-clusters under high-dose chemotherapy. Bolus administration acts as a nonselective annihilation process driving immune fields into an absorbing state, creating an immune-depleted vacuum enabling "Stochastic Pharmacokinetic Escape." Metronomic dosing and adjuvant immunotherapy can suppress this stochastic vulnerability window. Clinical data show most evaluable lesions exhibit nadir followed by regrowth; model fits reproduce this pattern, and the predicted demographic-noise scaling law (largest noise at smallest tumor volumes) is confirmed.
AI.conclusion: Deterministic notions of chemotherapy-induced cure are fundamentally incomplete: demographic fluctuations imply small residual tumor clusters always carry a nonzero relapse probability. The proposed stochastic framework provides quantitative, testable conditions under which alternative dosing strategies (metronomic) and adjuvant immunotherapy can mitigate this vulnerability, supported by clinical evidence.

title: Head Impact Characterization and Cellular Response of a Live-neuron cell-integrated Biomechanical Full-body Surrogate Model
summary: In this study, we develop a novel integrated framework that links the impact response with cellular dynamics using a live-neuron cell-integrated biomechanical full-body surrogate model. The impact event is simulated by allowing the surrogate model to fall from controlled seated release angles of 30-degree, 60-degree, and 90-degree. Three vertically stacked cell-culture Petri dishes, each containing live SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cells, were placed inside the head of a commercially available surrogate model. The dynamic response of the impact event was evaluated using acceleration measurements from six accelerometers, comprising three sensors mounted on the head surface and three embedded in series with the cell stacks, along with kinematic measurements of the fall and deformation of the head model. In parallel, an OpenSim-based modified musculoskeletal model was used to simulate the fall experiment. We found that variation in contact stiffness produced the largest change in the predicted head acceleration in the simulation. When the cellular response and the measured accelerations are compared, oxidative stress and cell viability showed trends consistent with the regional acceleration and angle of fall. At the 90-degree fall, where median peak linear accelerations ranged from 170-258g, and the maximum headform deformation was approximately 9.4 mm, oxidative stress increased to approximately twice that of the control sample. We also quantified the cellular drift of SH-SY5Y cells, which is focal in nature for the 90-degree impact condition. The corresponding fall scenarios were also simulated in OpenSim and a preliminary calibration relationship was developed to compare the kinematic responses of the physical surrogate and musculoskeletal model. Finally, the framework provides a basis for relating experimental surrogate measurements to human head-neck response during impact.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an integrated framework combining a live-neuron cell-integrated biomechanical full-body surrogate model with OpenSim musculoskeletal modeling to link impact biomechanics with cellular dynamics. Falling from 30°, 60°, and 90° angles, the surrogate head (containing SH-SY5Y cells) showed that contact stiffness most influenced predicted head acceleration, cellular oxidative stress and viability correlated with regional acceleration and fall angle, and the 90° fall produced ~2x oxidative stress with focal cell drift, establishing a calibration between physical and simulated responses.
AI.motivation: To bridge the gap between biomechanical impact responses (measured at the tissue/surrogate level) and cellular-level biological outcomes (such as oxidative stress and cell viability), enabling a more complete understanding of traumatic brain injury mechanisms.
AI.method: A full-body surrogate model with live SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cells in three stacked Petri dishes inside the head was dropped from 30°, 60°, and 90° seated release angles. Six accelerometers (three on head surface, three embedded with cell stacks) captured acceleration, while kinematic/deformation data were recorded. Parallel OpenSim musculoskeletal simulations modeled the falls, and cellular assays (oxidative stress, viability, drift) were correlated with mechanical measurements.
AI.result: Contact stiffness was the most influential parameter on predicted head acceleration. Cellular oxidative stress and viability trends matched regional acceleration and fall angle. At 90° (median peak linear accelerations 170-258g, max headform deformation ~9.4 mm), oxidative stress approximately doubled versus control, with focal cellular drift observed. OpenSim simulations enabled a preliminary calibration relationship between physical surrogate and musculoskeletal model kinematics.
AI.conclusion: The integrated experimental-simulation framework successfully links impact biomechanics with cellular dynamics, providing a basis for translating surrogate measurements to human head-neck response prediction during impact and supporting future TBI research.

title: The effect of the excitatory feedback in anticipated synchronization and phase bistability regimes in neuronal populations
summary:
Anticipated synchronization (AS), in which the receiver leads the sender and the phase lag is negative, can emerge in unidirectionally coupled dynamical systems when the receiver has faster internal dynamics than the sender. In cortical-like population models, AS and bistability between AS and delayed synchronization (DS) have been reported mainly in unidirectional motifs and have been proposed as possible explanations for phase relations observed in electrophysiological recordings. Because cortical areas are often connected bidirectionally, it is important to understand how excitatory feedback from the receiver to the sender affects the emergence and persistence of anticipatory synchronization and phase-bistable regimes.
  Here, we investigate the effect of the excitatory feedback on the phase relations between two cortical-like neuronal populations. We show that AS and phase bistability are not restricted to strictly unidirectional architectures, but remain robust in the presence of reciprocal coupling. In addition, we find that the transition from AS to DS can occur through different routes within the same motif, either via a bistable regime or via zero-lag synchronization, depending on the inhibitory coupling. More generally, the model exhibits a rich repertoire of phase relations, including: positive, negative, and zero-lag phase-lockings, as well as phase bistability, and phase-drift regimes.
  These results are consistent with the diversity of phase relations reported in electrophysiological experiments and suggest that fixed structural connectivity may support rapid reconfiguration of functional dynamics without requiring structural rewiring.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how excitatory feedback from receiver to sender affects anticipated synchronization (AS) and phase-bistable regimes in bidirectionally coupled cortical-like neuronal populations. The authors show AS and phase bistability remain robust under reciprocal coupling, reveal multiple transition routes from AS to delayed synchronization (DS), and demonstrate a rich repertoire of phase relations including positive, negative, zero-lag lockings, phase bistability, and phase drift.
AI.motivation: Cortical areas are often connected bidirectionally, yet previous studies of anticipated synchronization and phase-bistable regimes in cortical-like population models focused mainly on unidirectional motifs. Understanding how excitatory feedback affects these phenomena is important because they have been proposed as explanations for phase relations in electrophysiological recordings.
AI.method: The authors model two cortical-like neuronal populations with bidirectional coupling, where the receiver sends excitatory feedback to the sender. They systematically vary coupling parameters (including inhibitory coupling) and analyze the resulting phase relations between the two populations.
AI.result: AS and phase bistability remain robust with reciprocal coupling. The transition from AS to DS can occur via different routes within the same motif—either through a bistable regime or via zero-lag synchronization—depending on inhibitory coupling. The model exhibits a rich repertoire of phase relations including positive, negative, and zero-lag phase-lockings, phase bistability, and phase-drift regimes.
AI.conclusion: The results align with the diversity of phase relations observed in electrophysiological experiments. They suggest that fixed structural connectivity may support rapid reconfiguration of functional dynamics without requiring structural rewiring.

title: Characterising cardiac tissue properties with graph neural networks
comment: Accepted at The Statistical Atlases and Computational Modeling of the Heart (STACOM) workshop 2026
summary: Characterising electrophysiological properties of cardiac tissue efficiently and accurately from spatially sparse intracardiac measurements is clinically important for localising ablation targets and improving arrhythmia treatment. We developed a graph neural network-based framework trained on synthetic electrogram signals on 2D flat surfaces to identify areas of interest in the context of cardiac ablation for premature ventricular complexes (PVCs). Our method achieved an average precision of 0.96, 0.97, and 0.95 for the detection of single-patch fibrosis, rapid depolarisation and high excitability, respectively. The trained model can then be applied to 2D curved surfaces with few-shot fine-tuning, demonstrating its generalisation capability. Future work will develop this framework further for clinical use in PVC ablation.

AI.tldr: A graph neural network framework trained on synthetic electrogram signals from 2D flat surfaces identifies cardiac tissue regions of interest relevant to PVC ablation, achieving high average precision (0.95-0.97) for detecting fibrosis, rapid depolarisation, and high excitability, with few-shot fine-tuning enabling generalisation to curved surfaces.
AI.motivation: Efficiently and accurately characterising cardiac tissue electrophysiological properties from sparse intracardiac measurements is clinically important for localising ablation targets and improving arrhythmia treatment.
AI.method: Developed a graph neural network-based framework trained on synthetic electrogram signals on 2D flat surfaces to identify areas of interest for PVC ablation; uses few-shot fine-tuning for application to 2D curved surfaces.
AI.result: Achieved average precision of 0.96 for single-patch fibrosis, 0.97 for rapid depolarisation, and 0.95 for high excitability detection; demonstrated generalisation to curved surfaces via few-shot fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: The GNN framework shows strong potential for clinical use in PVC ablation, with future work aimed at further clinical development.

title: A Control-Theoretic Formulation of Global Workspace Theory
summary: Global workspace theory explains conscious access as the broadcasting of selected information to the rest of the network, but it lacks a formal criterion for identifying the mechanism that enables this access. We propose that a global workspace is a mediator, namely, a subnetwork that receives activity from distributed systems, transforms it through internal modes, and returns differentiated effects to the broader network. We formalize this claim as the Global Mediation Workspace (GMW), a control-theoretic formulation in which a candidate subnetwork is treated as an open system embedded in the remainder of the network. In this framework, reachability characterizes how the remainder can drive the candidate, observability characterizes how candidate states affect the remainder, and a boundary Hankel operator identifies the internal modes linking the two directions. The resulting signature quantifies mediation capacity, input-output alignment, effective dimensionality, and routed source-target breadth, each of which characterizes different components of global workspace. In synthetic benchmarks, we tested whether the signature can distinguish a planted differentiated mediator from dense hubs, one-sided receivers or broadcasters, and a split read/write aggregate with no common internal route. A nonlinear extension characterizes mediation through trajectory-conditioned differential operators, finite-amplitude response profiles, and state-dependent coalitions. As a preliminary application, we estimated the signature from ECoG recordings in four macaques under ketamine anesthesia. We found that input-output alignment was reduced during unconsciousness whereas potential capacity was increased. The GMW thus provides a formal and testable criterion for locating candidate global workspaces in neural recordings and for asking which aspects of mediation is crucial for conscious access.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Global Mediation Workspace (GMW), a control-theoretic framework that formalizes global workspace theory by defining a workspace as a mediator subnetwork. It uses reachability, observability, and a boundary Hankel operator to quantify mediation capacity, input-output alignment, effective dimensionality, and routed source-target breadth. The framework is validated on synthetic benchmarks and applied to ECoG recordings from macaques under ketamine anesthesia, showing reduced input-output alignment during unconsciousness.
AI.motivation: Global workspace theory explains conscious access as broadcasting of selected information but lacks a formal criterion for identifying the mechanism enabling this access. The authors seek to provide a testable, formal criterion for locating candidate global workspaces in neural systems.
AI.method: The paper formalizes the global workspace as a mediator subnetwork using control theory: reachability (how the remainder drives the candidate), observability (how candidate states affect the remainder), and a boundary Hankel operator identifying internal linking modes. This yields a signature quantifying mediation capacity, input-output alignment, effective dimensionality, and routed source-target breadth. A nonlinear extension uses trajectory-conditioned differential operators and state-dependent coalitions. The signature is tested on synthetic benchmarks and applied to macaque ECoG data under ketamine anesthesia.
AI.result: In synthetic benchmarks, the signature successfully distinguishes a planted differentiated mediator from dense hubs, one-sided receivers/broadcasters, and split read/write aggregates. In ECoG recordings from four macaques under ketamine anesthesia, input-output alignment was reduced during unconsciousness while potential capacity increased.
AI.conclusion: The GMW provides a formal, testable criterion for locating candidate global workspaces in neural recordings and enables asking which aspects of mediation are crucial for conscious access.

title: Phil Bourne (1953-2026): From Small Molecules to Big Data --- The Journey of a Multifaceted Visionary
summary: Born in London in 1953 and raised in Australia, Phil Bourne spent over four decades in science moving across scales: from crystal structures to the world's premier structural biology database; from scientific journals to national data policy; from molecules to institutions. The International Society for Computational Biology (ISCB) chose Phil to receive its 2026 Outstanding Service Award (Wiper, 2026). He passed away on 8 March 2026, in Charlottesville, Virginia, before he could receive it. This piece is in memory of Phil, who most recently served as the Founding Stephenson Dean of the University of Virginia's School of Data Science and as a Professor of Biomedical Engineering$\unicode{x2013}$and who was, over the course of his career, a steadfast builder of Computational Biology and Bioinformatics, of Open Science and Data Science. A tribute site, https://philbourne.muchloved.com, invites those who knew Phil to share memories, photos, and reflections.

AI.tldr: An obituary tribute to Phil Bourne, a pioneering computational biologist who was posthumously awarded the ISCB 2026 Outstanding Service Award for his four-decade career spanning structural biology, databases, journals, data policy, and institutions.
AI.motivation: To honor and memorialize Phil Bourne, a foundational figure in Computational Biology, Bioinformatics, Open Science, and Data Science, who passed away before receiving the ISCB 2026 Outstanding Service Award.
AI.method: This is a commemorative/obituary piece rather than a research paper; it narrates Bourne's career trajectory across scales—from crystal structures to major databases, from journals to national data policy, and from molecules to institution building.
AI.result: Phil Bourne's legacy is preserved through his contributions as a builder of computational biology, bioinformatics, open science, and data science, culminating in his role as Founding Stephenson Dean of UVA's School of Data Science.
AI.conclusion: Phil Bourne's passing represents a great loss to the scientific community, but his impact and contributions are enduring; a tribute site invites colleagues and friends to share memories.

title: Continual-learning rules shape representational drift
summary: Lifelong learning requires acquiring new knowledge without erasing the old. Yet neural population codes for familiar stimuli and behaviors change over days and weeks. This coexistence of stable memory and changing internal codes may depend on how a learning system prevents forgetting. We therefore tested whether different continual-learning mechanisms produce distinct patterns of representational drift. We trained convolutional networks on sequential image classification tasks and recurrent networks on sequences of cognitive tasks, tracking fixed probe representations across learning. Experience replay preserved earlier tasks in both architectures while representations drifted progressively with the number of intervening tasks. Drift was structured: later visual-processing stages and recurrent units' temporal tuning were especially labile, whereas coarse class organization and task-relevant temporal structure persisted. In contrast, algorithm that strongly anchored weights nearly froze representations. Directly anchoring an old representation during replay likewise suppressed drift and impaired acquisition of subsequent tasks. Together, these results link representational drift to the stability--plasticity trade-off: its magnitude is shaped by the mechanism that protects old knowledge, and suppressing it can restrict future learning. Drift may therefore provide an observable signature of the constraints that enable continual learning in brains and machines.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates how different continual-learning mechanisms (experience replay vs. weight anchoring) produce distinct patterns of representational drift in neural networks, showing that drift magnitude is linked to the stability-plasticity trade-off and may serve as an observable signature of continual learning constraints in both brains and machines.
AI.motivation: Lifelong learning requires balancing the acquisition of new knowledge with preserving old knowledge, yet neural population codes change over time (representational drift) even though memories persist. The authors aim to understand how different mechanisms that prevent forgetting shape the patterns of representational drift, linking drift to the stability-plasticity trade-off.
AI.method: The authors trained convolutional networks on sequential image classification tasks and recurrent networks on sequences of cognitive tasks. They tracked fixed probe representations across learning and compared experience replay versus strongly-anchoring weight algorithms. They analyzed drift structure by examining visual-processing stages, recurrent units' temporal tuning, coarse class organization, and task-relevant temporal structure.
AI.result: Experience replay preserved earlier tasks while representations drifted progressively with the number of intervening tasks. Drift was structured—later visual-processing stages and recurrent units' temporal tuning were especially labile, while coarse class organization and task-relevant temporal structure persisted. Strong weight anchoring nearly froze representations, and directly anchoring an old representation during replay suppressed drift but impaired acquisition of subsequent tasks.
AI.conclusion: Representational drift is linked to the stability-plasticity trade-off: its magnitude is shaped by the mechanism protecting old knowledge, and suppressing drift can restrict future learning. Drift may serve as an observable signature of the constraints enabling continual learning in both brains and machines.

title: tSymPerturb converts longitudinal symptom networks into time-indexed intervention strategies
summary: Longitudinal symptom networks encode directed prediction across measurement occasions, but outgoing connectivity does not by itself identify which symptom should be modified, how strongly it should be changed, or how a perturbation would propagate to later symptoms. We introduce tSymPerturb, a temporal extension of SymPerturb for cross-lagged panel networks (CLPNs). The framework separates source-state operators (temporal virtual knockout and knockdown), transition operators (directed edge and source-node communication blocking), and strategy procedures (dosage perturbation, combination analysis and sequence optimisation). For a two-wave linear CLPN, the central propagation identity is $Δμ_2 = B(μ_1 - μ_1^*)$, which makes the source time, outcome time and transition operator explicit. The formulation also yields three falsification constraints: dose response is exactly linear under a fixed linear transition model and linear dose map; independent source-state perturbations are additive at the mean level; and genuine treatment order is not identified from a single two-wave transition. In a known 22-node, four-module generating system, analytical temporal-knockout responses agreed with 250,000-draw Monte Carlo estimates within 0.0057 standard deviations. Across 200 independently generated datasets, median Spearman correlation with the population tVPPS ranking increased from 0.76 at n=250 to 0.88 at n=500 and 0.93 at n=1,000; median top-five recovery was 0.60, 0.80 and 0.80, respectively. Multi-wave simulations showed that target profiles can change across propagation horizons despite high overall rank concordance. tSymPerturb therefore converts longitudinal network structure into auditable, time-indexed intervention hypotheses while retaining the distinction between prediction and causal treatment effects.

AI.tldr: tSymPerturb extends SymPerturb to temporal cross-lagged panel networks, providing a framework for identifying which symptoms to modify and how perturbations propagate over time, with validated accuracy and falsification constraints.
AI.motivation: Longitudinal symptom networks can encode directed predictions across measurement occasions, but outgoing connectivity alone does not identify which symptom should be modified, how strongly it should be changed, or how a perturbation propagates to later symptoms. A systematic framework is needed for converting temporal network structure into intervention hypotheses.
AI.method: tSymPerturb separates source-state operators (temporal virtual knockout and knockdown), transition operators (directed edge and source-node communication blocking), and strategy procedures (dosage perturbation, combination analysis and sequence optimisation). For two-wave linear CLPNs, it uses the propagation identity Δμ2 = B(μ1 - μ1*) and yields three falsification constraints on dose response linearity, additivity, and treatment order identification.
AI.result: In a 22-node, four-module system, analytical temporal-knockout responses matched 250,000-draw Monte Carlo estimates within 0.0057 standard deviations. Across 200 datasets, median Spearman correlation with population tVPPS ranking rose from 0.76 (n=250) to 0.88 (n=500) and 0.93 (n=1,000); median top-five recovery was 0.60, 0.80, and 0.80. Multi-wave simulations showed target profiles vary across propagation horizons despite high rank concordance.
AI.conclusion: tSymPerturb converts longitudinal network structure into auditable, time-indexed intervention hypotheses while preserving the distinction between prediction and causal treatment effects.

title: KHiM-Mamba: Injecting Pathology Knowledge into Mamba via Hidden-State Modulation for Whole Slide Image Analysis
summary: Whole slide image analysis is commonly formulated as multiple instance learning (MIL), where instance features are contextually updated and aggregated into a slide representation, a process we term slide encoding dynamics. Recently, selective state-space models (SSM) have emerged as promising MIL architectures due to their long-sequence modeling capability and linear complexity. However, existing SSM-based MIL methods rely solely on visual features during MIL. Meanwhile, in large-scale WSIs, where sparse diagnostically decisive regions are surrounded by abundant irrelevant information, such purely vision-driven selective dynamics can misallocate state updates and readouts, causing the evolving SSM state to accumulate task-irrelevant evidence and dilute critical diagnostic cues over long scan trajectories. In this work, we propose the Knowledge-Aware Hidden-State Modulation architecture (KHiM-Mamba), which innovatively regulates Mamba's core selective state-space mechanism with explicit knowledge priors, steering slide encoding dynamics toward diagnostically meaningful evidence accumulation. Specifically, we redesign the original SSM layer to perform knowledge modulation operations during the evolution of hidden states, thereby guiding what visual evidence is accumulated and retrieved from the hidden state at each encoding step. Furthermore, we additionally introduce a local-adaptive vocabulary retrieval module that uses large language models to assign each patch fine-grained, tissue-specific semantic descriptions, enabling precise modulation across diverse tasks. Experiments on 11 public benchmarks across 4 tasks show that KHiM-Mamba consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance.

AI.tldr: KHiM-Mamba is a novel SSM-based multiple instance learning architecture for whole slide image analysis that regulates Mamba's selective state-space mechanism with explicit knowledge priors (tissue-specific semantic descriptions from LLMs) to guide hidden-state evolution toward diagnostically meaningful evidence, achieving SOTA results on 11 public benchmarks across 4 tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing SSM-based MIL methods for WSI rely purely on visual features, but in large-scale WSIs with sparse diagnostic regions surrounded by irrelevant tissue, purely vision-driven selective dynamics cause the SSM state to accumulate task-irrelevant evidence and dilute critical diagnostic cues over long scanning trajectories.
AI.method: KHiM-Mamba redesigns the SSM layer to perform knowledge modulation during hidden-state evolution, guiding what visual evidence is accumulated and retrieved at each encoding step. It also introduces a local-adaptive vocabulary retrieval module that uses LLMs to assign fine-grained, tissue-specific semantic descriptions to each patch for precise modulation across tasks.
AI.result: Experiments on 11 public benchmarks across 4 tasks demonstrate that KHiM-Mamba consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance.
AI.conclusion: Integrating explicit knowledge priors into Mamba's selective state-space mechanism effectively steers slide encoding dynamics toward diagnostically meaningful evidence, addressing the dilution problem of purely vision-driven approaches in large-scale WSI analysis.

title: Test-Time Instance Selection for Improved Whole Slide Image Analysis
comment: Accepted at The 2nd MICCAI Workshop on Efficient Medical AI (EMA4MICCAI 2026)
summary: Whole Slide Image (WSI) analysis has been widely studied for cancer diagnosis. Conventionally, a gigapixel WSI is divided into small patches and processed by Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) models. However, existing MIL models typically process all patches, many of which contain redundant or non-informative tissue patterns. Although recent approaches have focused on instance selection to identify discriminative patches and reduce redundancy, these selection modules still require additional training. In this work, we propose Test-Time Instance Selection (TTIS), a training-free, plug-and-play framework that selects compact yet representative patches during inference. TTIS further incorporates a multi-view ensemble strategy to integrate distinct facets of tissue morphology, enhancing robustness. Importantly, TTIS can be seamlessly integrated into existing MIL models without retraining or architectural changes, enabling flexible deployment. Extensive evaluations across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that our approach improves or matches baseline MIL performance across a range of classification and subtyping tasks. Our implementation code is available at https://github.com/QuIIL/TTIS

AI.tldr: TTIS is a training-free, plug-and-play test-time instance selection framework for Whole Slide Image analysis that selects compact yet representative patches during inference and uses a multi-view ensemble strategy, improving or matching baseline MIL performance across classification and subtyping tasks without retraining.
AI.motivation: Existing MIL models for WSI analysis process all patches including many redundant or non-informative ones, and recent instance selection approaches require additional training, limiting flexibility and deployment.
AI.method: TTIS proposes a training-free, plug-and-play framework that selects compact yet representative patches at inference time, and incorporates a multi-view ensemble strategy to integrate distinct facets of tissue morphology for enhanced robustness. It can be seamlessly integrated into existing MIL models without retraining or architectural changes.
AI.result: Extensive evaluations across multiple benchmarks show that TTIS improves or matches baseline MIL performance across a range of classification and subtyping tasks.
AI.conclusion: TTIS provides a flexible and training-free approach to instance selection in MIL-based WSI analysis that enhances or maintains performance while reducing redundancy, with implementation code made publicly available.

title: A Parameter-Free Few-Shot Evaluation for Elephant Vocalisation Classification
summary: We present a parameter-free episodic evaluation of nearest-centroid classification for elephant vocalisations on fixed pretrained acoustic embeddings, across the Elephant Voices (EV) and Linguistic Data Consortium (LDC) datasets. Rather than asking which embedding yields the best classifier when trained on all available labelled data, we ask how the simplest classifier performs as labelled exemplars per class are varied. Each class is represented by the mean of its support-set embeddings, and each query is assigned to the nearest centroid under squared Euclidean distance. We evaluate this centroid classifier on the Perch (ver. 1), Perch (ver. 2), and HuBERT (base, layer 2) embeddings, together with mel frequency cepstral coefficient (MFCC) features, in an N-way k-shot manner under the same cross-validation protocol as the trained baselines. A bootstrap over 100 resampled support sets quantifies the sampling noise. On the smaller, low-resource EV dataset, the centroid classifier using the stronger Perch (ver. 1) and Perch (ver. 2) embeddings overtakes the fully-trained logistic regression classifier from a single exemplar per class and the stronger recurrent classifier from two. Over the reduced set of call types on which the strongly-supervised end-to-end baseline was trained, the centroid classifier matches and then surpasses that baseline in mean average precision (mAP), from a few exemplars per class. On the larger LDC dataset, where labelled exemplars are abundant, the trained baselines retain their advantage at every k considered. At five exemplars per class, the centroid classifier using the strongest embedding, Perch (ver. 2), attains a mAP of 0.542 on the EV dataset and 0.368 on the LDC dataset. Parameter-free nearest-centroid classification is the stronger choice when labelled exemplars are few and the fixed embedding already encodes the features that separate the call types.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates parameter-free nearest-centroid classification on elephant vocalisations using pretrained embeddings (Perch v1/v2, HuBERT, MFCC) in an N-way k-shot framework across EV and LDC datasets. The centroid classifier outperforms trained baselines on the low-resource EV dataset from just 1-2 exemplars per class, while trained models retain advantages on the larger LDC dataset.
AI.motivation: To determine whether a simple, parameter-free classifier can rival or surpass heavily-trained baselines for elephant vocalisation classification when labelled exemplars are scarce, by systematically varying the number of support examples per class rather than assuming abundant labelled data.
AI.method: Nearest-centroid classification where each class is represented by the mean embedding of its support set, with queries assigned to the nearest centroid under squared Euclidean distance. Evaluated across Perch (v1), Perch (v2), HuBERT (base, layer 2) embeddings and MFCC features, in an N-way k-shot episodic framework with 100 bootstrap resamples of support sets, under the same cross-validation protocol as trained baselines.
AI.result: On the low-resource EV dataset, nearest-centroid with Perch embeddings beats fully-trained logistic regression from 1 exemplar per class and the stronger recurrent classifier from 2 exemplars, and matches/surpasses the end-to-end baseline in mAP. On the larger LDC dataset, trained baselines remain superior at all k. At k=5, the centroid classifier with Perch v2 achieves mAP of 0.542 (EV) and 0.368 (LDC).
AI.conclusion: Parameter-free nearest-centroid classification is the stronger choice when labelled exemplars are few and the fixed embedding already captures the discriminative features separating call types; trained models are preferable only when labelled data is abundant.

title: PathFinder: Joint Decompositions of Linked Multimodal Datasets
summary: Low-rank matrix decompositions can uncover patterns and structure in data and have a number of different applications across many disciplines. Extensions to "joint" low-rank decompositions have been proposed to link datasets from different modalities. While these methods enable the discovery of common patterns across modalities, they require that all the multimodal data share one or more dimensions. We propose a new analysis method, PathFinder, that enables co-analysis of datasets that do not necessarily all share a dimension. The key insight is that as long as pairs or subgroups of matrices do share some dimension, and that there are one or more paths that link across the data matrices, a global joint decomposition can be sought out. This enables the joint estimation of common patterns across different modalities, species, or scales, where a one-to-one mapping across all data along some dimension is not necessarily available. We show that PathFinder is a general umbrella under which many matrix decomposition methods fall as special cases. It can be used to discover common patterns across disparate datasets and to make predictions for missing data or modalities.

AI.tldr: PathFinder is a new analysis method for joint low-rank matrix decomposition that enables co-analysis of datasets that do not necessarily share all dimensions, as long as there are linking paths between data matrices. It generalizes many existing matrix decomposition methods and can discover common patterns across disparate datasets and predict missing data.
AI.motivation: Existing joint low-rank matrix decomposition methods require that all multimodal data share one or more common dimensions. This limitation prevents co-analysis of datasets that do not all share a dimension, such as data across different modalities, species, or scales.
AI.method: PathFinder leverages the key insight that as long as pairs or subgroups of matrices share some dimension and there exists one or more paths linking across the data matrices, a global joint decomposition can be sought out. This creates a general framework that unifies many existing matrix decomposition methods as special cases.
AI.result: PathFinder can discover common patterns across disparate datasets and make predictions for missing data or modalities. It serves as a general umbrella under which many matrix decomposition methods fall as special cases.
AI.conclusion: PathFinder expands the applicability of joint low-rank decomposition to datasets that do not necessarily share all dimensions, providing a general framework for cross-modal, cross-species, and cross-scale analyses.

title: CORAL: A Modality Invariant Framework for Robust Vital Sign Rate Estimation Using Correloform Analysis
comment: main manuscript: 11 pages, 2 tables, 4 figures supplemental materials: 25 pages, 4 tabes, 31 figures
summary: Heart rate and respiration rate are crucial vital signs. We present CORAL to address challenges in automating continuous vital sign monitoring 1) in-hospital across broader populations (age, disease states), 2) at-home in telehealth and wellbeing applications (noise, placement), and 3) across data modalities (ECG, PPG, SCG, BioZ, etc.). We re-introduce Short-Time Autocorrelation Functions (STACFs) to introduce the correloform - a highly interpretable 2D signal transformation for tracking periodicity over time - and define CORAL as a generic analytical framework for robust rate estimation of quasi-periodic signals. We rigorously benchmark CORAL to show ubiquitous application in biosignals via capabilities arising by mathematical construction rather than domain-specific engineering, including rate estimation, resilient noise handling, automatic channel selection, and signal quality indication. CORAL achieves excellent instantaneous noninvasive fetal HR agreement in FECGSYNDB (F1 = 0.999) and ADFECGDB (F1 = 1.000). With difficult NICU neonates, CORAL estimates RR from wearable BioZ at r = 0.858 against breath-interval RR from simultaneous wired Philips impedance. CORAL SCG HR on CEBS achieves r = 0.990 and in free-living activity r = 0.970 when compared against commercial ECG. Without QRS detection, CORAL's instantaneous HR agrees with Pan-Tompkins and NeuroKit2 detectors as closely as they agree with each other (MIMIC-IV ICU ECG r = 0.87 to each vs. 0.88 between them). CORAL's HR standard deviation correlates strongly with interval-based HRV SDNN, even from mechanical SCG (CEBS r = 0.733) and across an ICU ECG cohort (r = 0.768).

AI.tldr: CORAL is a generic analytical framework based on Short-Time Autocorrelation Functions (STACFs) and the "correloform" transformation for robust rate estimation of quasi-periodic biosignals, achieving excellent performance across ECG, PPG, SCG, BioZ modalities in both hospital and at-home settings without domain-specific engineering.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches to continuous vital sign monitoring face challenges across broader populations, noisy at-home settings, and diverse data modalities. Current methods often rely on domain-specific engineering rather than generalizable signal processing principles.
AI.method: CORAL re-introduces Short-Time Autocorrelation Functions (STACFs) to create the correloform, a 2D signal transformation tracking periodicity over time. This forms a generic analytical framework for estimating rates of quasi-periodic signals, providing capabilities such as rate estimation, noise resilience, automatic channel selection, and signal quality indication by mathematical construction.
AI.result: CORAL achieves F1=0.999 (FECGSYNDB) and F1=1.000 (ADFECGDB) for fetal HR; r=0.858 for RR from NICU BioZ; r=0.990 (CEBS) and r=0.970 (free-living) for SCG HR; HR agreement matching Pan-Tompkins/NeuroKit2 on MIMIC-IV; and strong HRV SDNN correlations from mechanical SCG (r=0.733) and ICU ECG (r=0.768).
AI.conclusion: CORAL demonstrates that a mathematically principled, generic framework can deliver state-of-the-art performance across diverse biosignals and settings, reducing the need for domain-specific engineering while offering interpretability through the correloform representation.

title: Growth-Induced Transitions in Viscoelastic Matter
summary: Growth is a fundamental process in living systems. Although the stress-deformation response of growing materials is often described as either purely elastic or purely viscous, many biological tissues, from biofilms to tumors, exhibit both elastic and viscous behavior. Here, we show that this viscoelastic response can crucially control the mechanics of proliferating matter when the growth rate becomes comparable to the rate of stress relaxation. Focusing first on the prototypical case of a growing elastic beam, we find that the dynamics are governed by a single dimensionless parameter, $g τ$, where $g$ is the growth rate and $τ$ is the viscoelastic relaxation time. While the limits $g τ\to 0$ and $g τ\to \infty$ recover purely viscous and purely elastic behavior, respectively, the intermediate regime is not merely a smooth crossover between them. Instead, qualitatively new dynamics emerge at $g τ\sim 1$, including rapid transitions between metastable states that occur in neither limiting regime. We then develop a general, growth-compatible theoretical framework in which unconstrained growth is intrinsically stress-free, extending the analysis to other prototypical geometries and enabling simulations of more realistic growing biological materials. Within this framework, sharp mechanical transitions arise when stress generated by exponential growth accumulates faster than it can be dissipated by viscoelastic relaxation.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how viscoelasticity controls the mechanics of proliferating biological materials when growth rates are comparable to stress relaxation rates, revealing that intermediate regimes (gτ ~ 1) produce qualitatively new dynamics—including rapid transitions between metastable states—that occur in neither purely viscous nor purely elastic limits. The authors develop a growth-compatible theoretical framework where unconstrained growth is intrinsically stress-free, enabling analysis across prototypical geometries and simulations of realistic growing biological tissues.
AI.motivation: Biological tissues (biofilms, tumors) exhibit both elastic and viscous behavior, yet growth mechanics are often modeled as purely one or the other. The authors aim to understand how viscoelasticity fundamentally alters the mechanics of proliferating matter, particularly when growth and stress relaxation timescales interact.
AI.method: The authors analyze a growing viscoelastic beam as a prototypical system, identifying a single dimensionless parameter gτ (growth rate × relaxation time) governing dynamics. They then develop a general theoretical framework in which unconstrained growth is intrinsically stress-free, extending the analysis to other geometries and enabling simulations.
AI.result: The intermediate regime (gτ ~ 1) exhibits qualitatively new dynamics not seen in either limiting case, including rapid transitions between metastable states. The framework shows sharp mechanical transitions arise when exponentially accumulated stress outpaces viscoelastic dissipation.
AI.conclusion: Viscoelasticity crucially controls growing matter mechanics, and the regime where growth rate matches stress relaxation produces emergent behaviors that cannot be captured by purely elastic or purely viscous descriptions of biological materials.

title: Population Structure Analysis of an Inbred Population using Quantitative Shape Phenotyping from Stereo Retinal Photographs
summary: The population structure of an inbred population of 781 people on Norfolk Island in the Pacific, 318 of which are descendants of the original Mutineers of the Bounty, is analyzed phenotypically using shape from stereo retinal fundus photographs. Three-dimensional optic nerve head (ONH) shape is reconstructed from stereo pairs by a multi-scale stereo matching algorithm. Using deep neural network, the shape of ONH, which is under genetic control, is decomposed into a set of hierarchical features through self-taught learning. Features captured at different levels are selected according to their discriminant power in identifying the two populations. The prediction accuracy is evaluated with stratified cross validation. Given the selected feature set, individuals are grouped into k hierarchical clusters and cluster membership fractions are determined for k=2,3,4,5,6,7. Population structure analysis on the basis of phenotypes through image analysis allows heritability and linkage analysis, including founder effects from English and Polynesian ancestors, potentially leading to new genetic risk factors for glaucoma and other ONH-related eye diseases.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes genetic population structure in an inbred Norfolk Island population by reconstructing 3D optic nerve head (ONH) shape from stereo retinal photographs, extracting hierarchical features via deep neural networks, and clustering individuals to distinguish descendants of Bounty mutineers from other populations for potential glaucoma genetic research.
AI.motivation: To identify genetic risk factors for glaucoma and other ONH-related eye diseases by leveraging a unique inbred population with known founder effects (English and Polynesian ancestors), using phenotype-based population structure analysis as a proxy for genetic analysis.
AI.method: 3D ONH shape is reconstructed from stereo retinal fundus photographs using a multi-scale stereo matching algorithm. Deep neural networks perform self-taught learning to decompose ONH shape into hierarchical features. Features are selected by discriminant power for distinguishing the two populations. Prediction accuracy is evaluated via stratified cross-validation, and individuals are clustered into k hierarchical clusters (k=2-7) to determine population structure.
AI.result: The approach successfully decomposes ONH shape into hierarchical features that discriminate between the two populations, and population structure is revealed through hierarchical clustering with cluster membership fractions determined across k=2 to 7 clusters.
AI.conclusion: Phenotype-based population structure analysis via image analysis enables heritability and linkage analysis, including founder effects, potentially uncovering new genetic risk factors for glaucoma and other ONH-related diseases.

title: Multi-Feature Riemannian Hypergraph for Online Test-Time Adaptation of Motor Imagery Brain-Computer Interface
summary: In clinical motor imagery brain-computer interface (MI-BCI) decoding, cross-day transferability and online operation remain two critical challenges. Hypergraphs can improve transferability by capturing higher-order sample relationships, yet existing hypergraph-based methods for online emotion recognition neglect the cross-day benefits of Riemannian geometry widely adopted in EEG transfer learning. To bridge this gap, we propose the Multi-feature Riemannian Hypergraph (MRieHy), a framework tailored for online test-time adaptation in MI-BCI decoding that leverages Riemannian geometry to strengthen cross-day transferability. MRieHy first computes Riemannian means of covariance matrices from cross-day training data to align multi-day distributions. It then constructs a hypergraph over covariance matrices using Riemannian distance, complemented by a second hypergraph over deep features built with cosine similarity. The two hypergraphs are fused via adaptively learned combination weights, jointly optimized with the label projection matrices. During online testing, MRieHy maintains a first-in-first-out buffer of recent samples, performs Riemannian alignment on the buffered data, and decodes with the learned hypergraph. Extensive experiments on a private four-class ECoG dataset and two public four-class EEG datasets validate that MRieHy achieves notable performance gains over state-of-the-art baselines.

AI.tldr: MRieHy is a novel framework for online motor imagery brain-computer interface decoding that combines Riemannian geometry with hypergraph learning to achieve cross-day transferability and online test-time adaptation, demonstrating superior performance over state-of-the-art baselines on ECoG and EEG datasets.
AI.motivation: Two critical challenges in MI-BCI decoding are cross-day transferability and online operation. Existing hypergraph-based methods for emotion recognition ignore the benefits of Riemannian geometry for EEG transfer learning, leaving a gap in combining these approaches for online MI-BCI decoding.
AI.method: MRieHy computes Riemannian means of covariance matrices from cross-day training data for multi-day distribution alignment, constructs a Riemannian-distance-based hypergraph over covariance matrices plus a cosine-similarity-based hypergraph over deep features, fuses them via adaptively learned weights with label projection matrices, and employs a first-in-first-out buffer with Riemannian alignment during online testing.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on a private four-class ECoG dataset and two public four-class EEG datasets demonstrate notable performance gains over state-of-the-art baselines.
AI.conclusion: The proposed MRieHy framework effectively bridges Riemannian geometry and hypergraph learning to enhance cross-day transferability and enable online test-time adaptation in MI-BCI decoding, outperforming existing methods.

title: PertMind: Eliciting Emergent Biological Reasoning in LLM via Reinforcement Learning on Cellular Perturbation Data
comment: Project page: https://shapsider.github.io/PertMind/ Code: https://github.com/shapsider/PertMind Model: https://huggingface.co/tzcfly/PertMind
summary: Large language models can describe mechanisms, yet scalable post-training still depends on costly, manually curated biological reasoning traces. Here we show that cellular perturbation atlases can instead become reinforcement-learning environments, where measured gene responses provide computable rewards for biological reasoning. We introduce PertMind, which combines trusted-trajectory supervised initialization with gene-, pathway-, and format-level reinforcement signals. Trained only on forward perturbation-response prediction, PertMind improved response inference in unseen cellular contexts while retaining general language capabilities. It also transferred without task-specific post-training to reverse perturbation identification, double-perturbation reasoning, phenotypic-screen prioritization, and biological-process interpretation. PertMind further generated biological profiles that supported competitive gene, cell, and donor representations across multiscale downstream tasks. These results support the hypothesis that reinforcement on experimental endpoints can concentrate reusable biological strategies already accessible to pretrained models. More broadly, perturbation-derived reinforcement learning offers a scalable route for transforming expanding experimental atlases into training environments for general-purpose biological reasoning.

AI.tldr: PertMind uses cellular perturbation atlases as reinforcement-learning environments, where measured gene responses serve as computable rewards for training LLMs on biological reasoning. Combined with supervised initialization on trusted trajectories and multi-level reinforcement signals, it improves perturbation-response prediction in unseen contexts while retaining general language capabilities, and transfers to multiple downstream biological tasks without task-specific post-training.
AI.motivation: Scalable post-training of LLMs for biology is bottlenecked by costly, manually curated biological reasoning traces. The authors seek an alternative scalable training signal derived from experimental data rather than human curation.
AI.method: PertMind combines (1) supervised initialization on trusted biological reasoning trajectories, (2) reinforcement signals at gene-, pathway-, and format-levels, using measured gene responses from cellular perturbation atlases as computable rewards for forward perturbation-response prediction.
AI.result: PertMind improved response inference in unseen cellular contexts, retained general language capabilities, and transferred zero-shot to reverse perturbation identification, double-perturbation reasoning, phenotypic-screen prioritization, and biological-process interpretation. It also generated biological profiles supporting competitive gene, cell, and donor representations across multiscale downstream tasks.
AI.conclusion: Reinforcement on experimental endpoints can concentrate reusable biological strategies already present in pretrained models. Perturbation-derived RL offers a scalable route to transform expanding experimental atlases into training environments for general-purpose biological reasoning.

title: Order-Sensitive Fast-Synapse Limits in Sparse Excitatory-Inhibitory Threshold-Reset Networks
summary: Componentwise weak convergence of signed synaptic kernels does not, by itself, determine the fast-synapse limit of a sparse threshold-reset network. Within a causal event protocol with clamped refractoriness and smooth positive-delay kernels, we construct two families whose excitatory and inhibitory measures converge weakly to $δ_0$ while their microscopic arrival orders are reversed. A target fires in the excitatory-first family and not in the inhibitory-first family precisely when $x+a-b<θ\le x+a$. Strict margins preserve this response under perturbations of the target state, aggregate E/I pulse masses, and bounded drift. The macroscopic effect persists on a moderately sparse Dale-compatible random block graph with $q_N\to\infty$ and $q_N/N\to0$. The two systems share their graph and initial data. Along every deterministic joint scale $\varepsilon_N\downarrow0$, their population-averaged firing counts differ by $1/2+o_{L^1}(1)$. A bounded-degree construction and a later probe show that the discrepancy is macroscopic and can persist through reset. Fixed positive-delay kernels with finitely many classes admit a stable regime. Before grazing, typewise-mixing sparse networks converge to a delayed class mean-field system.
